Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned at six o'clock yesterday evening I had referred to reports made by the combines investigation branch and tabled in the house since 1945. I had just mentioned the report tabled in 1945 on Canada and international cartels, which did not contain any specific reference to any offence under the combines legislation in Canada.
I shall now refer to some reports which have been made on Canadian industries since that time and which have been tabled in this house. In July of 1947 there was a report on dental supplies. In April of 1948 there was a report on an investigation into optical goods. In both those cases the combines investigation branch found there was a conspiracy in restraint of trade. In the first one prosecution failed on a procedural ground, and in the second case I believe prosecution was not started because of the decision made in the first one, the circumstances in both cases being similar.

In 1948 there was an investigation into the baking industry in the western provinces and the report was tabled in that year. The companies were convicted in Calgary in October, 1951. I should like the members of this house to pay attention to some of the statements made by the presiding judge, Mr. Justice McBride of Alberta, when giving his judgment in the case. The justice said the bakers were more interested in price than in quality, service and salesmanship. Bread is an item of necessity that goes into every home. Even in the most poverty-stricken homes they cannot get along without their daily supply of bread. But here in this important industry-shall I call it an industry?- it was found that there was a combine. I am reading now from a report in the Winnipeg Tribune of October 3, 1951, which contains the following:
Mr. Justice McBride referred in his judgment to certain actions of the six companies. This included illegitimate use of Alberta government stationery. He termed this a "fraudulent system ... a system of misrepresentation and fraud, a system of plunder comparable to meeting a man on the street and forcibly robbing him of his money."
In our courts we are quite severe with those who hold up people on the streets and rob them of their money, but while there was a conviction in this case and fines imposed I do not have much doubt that the same procedure for exploiting consumers is being carried on today, in the same way as in 1948 and previous years before the investigation took place.

This was the report that pretty nearly unhorsed the Minister of Justice (Mr. G-arson) when he came down here as a tenderfoot from the Portage plains. There was no prosecution in this case because I understand that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said "No". In 1949 there was a report on the match companies and they were convicted in Montreal in May of 1951. I understand the case is under appeal. Five match companies were involved and a monopoly was proven. The trial was conducted by Mr. Justice Bienvenue-I hope I am pronouncing his name correctly-in Montreal, and he gave quite an extensive judgment. It took him nearly two hours to read it. A report in the Ottawa Journal of October 29, 1951, contains the following with respect to Mr. Justice Bienvenue's findings:
His conclusion was that the Eddy Company succeeded, by itself or with other accused corporations, in forming and operating an illegal agreement from 1927 to 1950 . . . The fact that Eddy Match finally found itself alone in the wooden match industry was not accidental, Mr. Justice Bienvenue said, but was what it wanted after having taken the means to bring it about . . . Mr. Justice Bienvenue reviewed in detail the methods used in the formation of the monopoly, including setting resale prices for jobbers, establishing "fighting brands"-
Whatever that may mean.
*-controlling prices and giving special discounts.
Mr. Justice Bienvenue said it was no wonder that the financial situation of the Eddy Company had always been excellent and that it had paid substantial dividends in bad years as well as good since its incorporation. There is not much free competition there.
In 1952 there was a report on the rubber companies. Indeed, it is a composite of six inquiries and included investigations into mechanical rubber goods, tires, tubes and accessories, and rubber footwear. The rubber companies did not wait to be convicted. They pleaded guilty and were sentenced in court a few days ago. I have before me a news item from the Ottawa Journal of November 23, 1953, which reports the judge's decision. Mr. Justice Schroeder said:
It is hard to understand how firms otherwise reputable and honest in their dealings could be so conscienceless.
It was said that these companies had carried on an illegal combine for 15 years. I do not know of any hold-up man who has been able to carry on that long without being caught and convicted. The special crown prosecutor,

Mr. T. N. Phelan, estimated that the companies illegally extracted $1,300,000 a year for the 15 years during which the companies had combined. The amount of the fine was put in the paper in large type and was $170,000. I have figured that in the 15 years at $1,300,000 a year these companies illegally extracted $19,500,000 from the consumers of Canada.
Maybe a fine of $170,000 was all that could be imposed under the law but I feel sure that the amount is not sufficient to help the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) bring about free competition in this industry. Something should be done to help him, because he is going to have a very hard time as things look now. Just yesterday the Minister of Justice laid on the table the report of the investigation into the electrical wire and cable industry. In this case ten companies, according to the investigator, had been carrying on an illegal price fixing combine for 41 years. I imagine the reason they did not carry it on before that was that they were not all in business prior to that time. Yet we have people like the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton), who spoke yesterday afternoon, objecting to government planning. He wants planning by private enterprise. In view of all these investigations, what does private enterprise plan for? It plans for its own pockets and nothing else.
I have been trying to tell that to members of the house for the last 23 years, and I am glad the Department of Justice, through the work being carried on by the combines investigation branch, is now helping to impress it upon hon. members. There are quite a number of other investigations, but I have not time to deal with all of them in detail. There have been investigations into fine papers, coarse papers and the resale price maintenance of soap products. In the latter case I think the minister said the other day that if the companies would not do it again they would not be prosecuted this time. Then there has been an investigation into price discrimination between hardware dealers in North Bay. Again I believe the Minister of Justice said that if they would be good fellows he would let them go. He is going to give them another chance.
I have noticed that the members to my right do not like socialism, not even when it comes in a silk hat. It may be that they are justified in not liking it in a silk hat. I am not sure that I would like it in a silk hat, because it is not likely to be the genuine thing. However, it might be. Circumstances and the pressure of events are pretty strong persuasive factors.
I should like to ask the Leader of the Opposition and others sitting to my right, the members of the government and also those

If they have, this is what they have found; that every one of these countries has either a socialist government, or has had a socialist government and now has a strong socialist opposition.

I am reading from an editorial which appeared in the New York Herald Tribune of February 9, 1948. The Herald Tribune is not a socialist newspaper:
The true allies of democracy in Europe are the socialist parties. They alone give us any hope for the preservation of personal liberty. We have systematically despised and underestimated them . . .
The same as has been done in this country.
. . . just because we do not want socialism here at home. We have never taken the trouble to understand the historical development of these parties. They alone are capable of forming strong democratic states, and if they perish, the hope of democracy will perish with them.
This is not just something I am saying. It is something that must be apparent to anybody who will take the time to look over the world and see what is happening. Which are the nations that are causing us worry in Europe? Compare Italy, where there is no socialist party or a very weak one, with Sweden where a socialist party has been administering affairs for the last 25 or 30 years, or with Norway or Denmark; or compare Great Britain, where there has been a socialist party, with France.
I do not want to put a plug in for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), but when I hear my friends to my right talking about high taxes I think there is something worse than high taxes that can happen to a country. That is when a country has a government that is afraid to tax, and by being afraid to tax the right people, those who should be taxed, they are inviting a revolution that will take away with violence and confusion more than would be taken away by orderly taxation.
In conclusion I would like to tell my friend once again that time is running out, and that this is not the time for basing our actions on preconceived ideas and bias inherited from the past. We are living in a new age when new developments are taking place every day, and each new development is demanding new changes and new attitudes toward the way in which we make our living.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate opened two weeks ago today, and a most extraordinary thing has happened which I must confess surprises me very much. That is that during this whole period the subject of defence has not so far been mentioned. Perhaps I should simply be grateful for this and remain discreetly silent, but I believe that it is a fact that defence is by all odds the largest single business in the country today. The fact that we have some 20,000 Canadians serving abroad in seven different countries, the fact that defence takes about 50 per cent of the national budget and 10 per cent of the national income, the fact that in one way or another about 10 per cent of the Canadian people are engaged directly or indirectly in our national defence, all demand that this house and the people have from time to time reports on progress; that an indication be given of what has been achieved, of what lies ahead, and of some of the problems that have arisen.
On that account I make no apology for intervening in this debate at this or any other time to defend the armed forces when they need defence, to accept responsibility and blame when that is due-and that I have had to do-but above everything else to make it as plain as can be that this huge operation in which we are involved is something vitally important to all of us and to all the people of Canada. Unless we have that comprehension, and unless we see something of the implications of what is involved in the whole operation, then matters are likely to get out of perspective.
Above everything else, and more dangerous than everything else, the men who are serving us abroad are apt to be forgotten, the cause which we are aiming to preserve is apt to be lost sight of, and the whole defence effort here, as in other countries, is likely to lose the momentum with which it was started some three or four years ago. Consequently today I think I should, in so far as time permits, say something about Korea, the build-up of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and, perhaps the most urgently required, make as full a statement as possible on the subject of continental defence.

Since the cessation of hostilities in Korea on July 27 a good many of us are apt to forget what was involved in the three long years of that agonizing war. We are apt to forget how the tide of battle swept up and down that 800-mile long peninsula almost three times, and how at times the outlook for the United Nations forces was desperate indeed. But in the end they succeeded, and succeeded completely, in achieving the military objective of the Korean war, which was to stop the aggressor; and it had no other objective from the military point of view. This was the first time, I believe, in the history of the world that 16 nations, because they had signed an agreement in the charter of the United Nations, joined together in armed action to stop aggression. It was the first time that nations had acted together in peace as an international force along lines somewhat similar to those along which the police forces of our civilian communities operate to stop armed robbery and prevent crime. The objective was not victory. The objective was to prevent aggression by stopping aggression.
For that reason at times the war and its results have not appeared spectacular; nonetheless the objective was just as great a one as the objective of victory in a war, and the objective was achieved just as definitely from the military point of view as it could have been had victory been achieved in a war.
On that account I believe we members of the United Nations should congratulate ourselves that, under the leadership of the United States, we had the collective intention and the collective will to work together in unison to restore peace and to bring about a condition of order. In this work the officers and men of the Canadian forces participating-the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force-played a fair share in bringing about that great result. And on that account, as was said by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), they deserve our gratitude for their service.
There have been several by-products of this operation which have been interesting indeed. One is that it has been established that 16 nations can work together effectively in a theatre of war far away from their own countries, that they can have several supply lines operating simultaneously, and that they can accept without jealousy the leadership of the most powerful nation of their group, the United States.
The great success achieved by the commonwealth division reflects credit on its leaders, and particularly its first commanding

officer, then Major General and now Lieutenant General Sir A. J. H. Cassels, who was more than a great soldier in the field. He exercised his command with foresight and tact, and even with statesmanship, because he was the leader of what was virtually an independent force, though serving under United Nations command.
He was succeeded by another fine soldier, Major General West. The six nations of the commonwealth, co-operating in the commonwealth division, worked together harmoniously-more effectively, I think, and in a more friendly way than we knew in either the first or second world wars.
As for our own brigade, it had good leadership in the persons of Brigadier Rockingham, Brigadier Bogert and, for the closing days, Brigadier Jean Allard. The officers and men of the 25th Canadian infantry brigade earned the high repute in which they were held. On that front, like the commonwealth division, they were recognized by everyone as second to none.
Further it was most heartening to see the way in which the various units of the Canadian brigade there, and the supporting units, worked together and side by side with the representatives of other nations. The number of Canadians taking part was 22,000. Altogether they had a total of 1,558 casualties, of which 304 are either dead or presumed to be dead, 39 died of wounds, six are still missing, 32 are returned prisoners of war, and 97 died from ordinary causes. I might add that, so far as we know, all Canadian prisoners of war were returned.
These casualties are serious, as indeed all casualties always are. We regret them, and extend deepest sympathy to the next of kin of those who were killed. However, I think it is fair to say that, having regard to the fierceness of the fighting and the fact that it was carried on over a period of three years, we can express some satisfaction that the casualties were not higher. I believe we may have that satisfaction, always keeping in mind the nature of the country, the fierceness of the fighting and its duration.
This, I believe, can be credited in part to good leadership and the fact that, almost without exception, all our men arrived fully trained. They were well equipped and kept up to strength. Another important factor was that, unlike most of the other nations, we were able to carry out rotation by units, so that the second battalions of the R.C.R.'s and the P.P.C.L.I.'s and the Van Doos which went out first were replaced by the first battalions and the first battalions by the third battalions; each unit arriving as a group, and fighting together under leadership that they learned to respect in Canada.
The Address-Mr. Claxton
This is far more expensive in manpower, of course, than rotation by individuals. But we believe that it is the right way to do it, and we are very happy that it was possible to do it that way. I may say that we are following the same course in connection with the rotation of units in Germany.
The Royal Canadian Navy did its share with eight ships participating in fifteen tours of duty. They steamed the astonishing total of 700,000 miles, and fired 130,000 shells, more I believe than our navy fired in action in the second world war. The role of the navy was largely that of acting as advance artillery up the west coast of Korea, and in doing so they made a great name for themselves. Their operations were carried out 8,000 miles from the base at Esqui-malt and 13,000 miles from that at Halifax. Altogether 3,621 officers and men of the navy took part in these Far Eastern operations.
The Royal Canadian Air Force carried on its heavy transport operations to the Far East with the aircraft of 426 transport squadron equipped with North Star aircraft. Altogether they made over a thousand Pacific crossings, flying some 36,000 hours for a total of 6,500,000 miles. They completed this great task over this long period of time, and through some of the most difficult flying country in the world, without loss or injury to aircraft, crew or passengers.
Altogether a total of 26,733 Canadians served in the Far East in the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force. It is estimated-and I think this figure will surprise hon. members- that of the 107,000 officers and men in the regular forces of Canada today, 20 per cent wear proudly on their breasts the ribbons of service with the United Nations and the commonwealth brigade in the Far East. So that virtually one out of five in the Canadian armed forces today, wherever they may be, is a veteran of Korea. He is an experienced and trained man, up to the minute in his knowledge of that type of warfare, confident of the ability of his service, his unit and himself to carry out any task given to him.
Altogether they have won 250 decorations, and have been mentioned in dispatches or received the Queen's commendation a similar number of times. At a later stage of the session, as is the practice, I shall ask the permission of the house to put on Hansard a list of those receiving decorations. Also, of course, a considerable number of those who served have left the regular forces and are to be found either in the ranks of the reserve forces or are available-those who are still physically fit-as trained reserves for duty at a moment's notice.

speechtext:
It would be between 6,000 and 7,000. That is the calculation I make from the figures I have already mentioned. The cost of this operation to Canada is very difficult to estimate. It depends on what you include; but taking into consideration the expenditures that have been made outside of Canada the total cost is about $200 million, of which some $50 million was paid to the United States for the supplies they furnished to us. We of course paid for everything we got, on a basis that was worked out very exactly with them.
If you take into account the indirect costs and add in a fair and proper proportion of the overhead for administration and training in respect of this force abroad and its training in Canada you might easily arrive at a cost to Canada of the Korean war, three, four or five times as great; but the direct cost for expenditures made on the war was approximately $200 million.
We had serving with us in Japan and later in Korea a number of Canadian Red Cross workers, and they did good work, for which I am now very glad to express the gratitude of the armed forces. Altogether there were 32 of them.
This was a very big undertaking for the United Nations, and particularly for the United States. We feel that that undertaking was justified; that had we not gone in for it and stopped aggression there, by this time there might have been aggression anywhere else. This was the first collective effort to stop the communists. It succeeded, and by its success we hope it will have made a lasting contribution to the security of all of us and to peace, which is our primary objective.
Simultaneously with this operation in Korea there the North Atlantic Treaty Organization came into existence. I should remind hon. members that that treaty had been in existence only a little more than four years, and that the build-up of the organization really started with plans agreed to at Washington just three years ago last month, so the period of the build-up of NATO in Europe and elsewhere corresponded closely with the period of the Korean war, and the countries included in both were faced with the challenge of doing both operations at the same time.
The build-up of forces in Europe has proceeded, though not as well as had been planned at the outset. The plan has not proved to be unrealistic. I am happy to be able to say that Canada has completed all her commitments to NATO either at or in advance of the due date.

The Canadian Army sent first the 27th brigade, and that brigade in its training, record and exercises made a reputation for military competency which I do not think has ever been matched-certainly it has never been excelled in peacetime-by any Canadian forces. I have never seen such praise given to a unit for its military competence as has been given to the 27th Canadian infantry brigade. That brigade has now returned home, and its place has been taken by the 1st Canadian infantry brigade. This brigade consists in part of men who have already seen service in Korea, and to a very great degree it is fully trained, up to strength and consists of seasoned, experienced soldiers. So while it will have a hard job to do in living up to the reputation the 27th brigade made for itself, I believe the previous records of those units that have served in Korea-[DOT] and part of this has served in Korea-will indicate that the name of Canada will be well upheld there.
This brigade is taking up its quarters at new camps that have been built for us by the Germans in the neighbourhood of Soest; that is, halfway between Hanover and Bonn in a very attractive part of Germany. They are near the Mohne See, which is a very beautiful artificial lake and reservoir, which hon. members may recall was the scene of the gallant operation of the dambusters.
These camps are four in number. They have permanent buildings, and we will be adding as soon as we can recreation rooms and buildings and accommodation for married personnel. We have made arrangements with the German government under which it will build for us at its expense a number of married quarters, recreation buildings, schools and other similar accommodation. They are to provide the buildings, the services and most of the maintenance and operation, in return for which we shall pay an annual rent estimated at 10 per cent of the capital cost, which should run to a total of $25 million, or about $2,500,000 a year for us.
During the year we have established an appropriate base depot at Antwerp under arrangements with the Belgian government, and that is in operation. We have moved that base from Hamburg, where it was, to the much more suitable location at Antwerp. Now we have completed the army part of our contribution to NATO.
The air force build-up has proceeded steadily and well in advance of the planned dates, beginning with three squadrons located at North Luffenham, followed by three more at Grostenquin, three more at Zweibrucken, and three more at Soellingen. The wing at North

Luffenham will move to Marville when the airfield there is completed, making a total of twelve constituting the air division which with its headquarters at Metz is fully operational. It is equipped with F-86E Sabre fighters and is, as everyone knows, one of the most formidable fighting forces in Europe today.
These operations of the air force have involved a very large-scale job of transportation of aircraft overseas. The first three squadrons were taken on H.M.C.S. Magnificent; the last nine flew across in a series of operations called "leapfrogs"-one, two, three, four-and I am happy to say that these were also completed without loss. This required a great deal of organization, monitoring of ships with accompanying aircraft, providing patrol ships, navigational aids, stores at every landing point, and so on. I might indicate to hon. members something of the complexities and niceties of this operation when I say that on some of the legs the Sabre fighters arrived at their destination with less than 10 minutes of fuel left. So there was not much time to go anywhere else.
The Royal Canadian Navy has continued its build-up of ships to meet its commitments to SACLANT, and that has been carried on. We expect that we will be able to meet our peacetime commitments to SACLANT, as in the case of the other services, but in the navy there is still some distance to go. We are up to date with those we have furnished, but plenty of target dates have not yet arrived and we hope to meet them.
The navy, like the air force and the army, have taken part in extensive exercises and operations with other NATO countries, indicating that NATO is now a formation of trained combat units, equipped and skilled and having the leadership, communications and other necessities for combined operations. This is a very different situation from what it was three years ago.
I*t can be said that while NATO is not yet close to achieving its final target, it has built up sufficient strength in Europe to add greatly to the capacity of Europe to defend itself and give time for reserves to be deployed and also for the movement of weapons of all kinds, so that the primary objective of NATO can be said to have been achieved. But there is no end to any military objective. The build-up must continue, and it has had to be related to the facts and possibilities, military, economic and financial, of the NATO countries so it could make steady progress toward the desired goal.
In concluding this part of my remarks I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the situation regarding Canadian 83276-24
The Address-Mr. Claxton soldiers, sailors and airmen overseas. Today we have 20,000 personnel of the regular forces located in seven countries outside of Canada. There are about 7,500 in the Far East; over 400 in the United States; nearly 2,000 in the United Kingdom; about 100 in Belgium; 1,500 in France and over 7,500 in Germany. That represents today about one-fifth of the total regular strength of the Canadian armed forces.
You can imagine that this presents many problems, problems which Canada has not had to face before in peacetime. For example, with regard to the personnel alone, we have problems arising out of rotation, transportation, accommodation, training, welfare, educational services, the provision of chapels, married quarters, schools and stores. We will soon have located in Germany and France a number of little communities of Canadian service personnel with their wives and children. They are dependent upon the armed forces for what they need in the way of accommodation, schooling, religious and other services, and everything that goes or should go into making up normal community life. To provide this is quite a difficult operation in Canada, but you can imagine how difficult it is to carry on abroad, not only in view of the distances and the diverse conditions in those countries but also having regard to matters like civil and criminal jurisdiction, customs and excise taxes, postal and immigration regulations and all the other things that affect the servicemen, but affect still more the civilians accompanying service units. We have to work out arrangements with all the foreign governments concerned to arrive at satisfactory agreements regarding all these points. I am happy to say that these agreements have either been made or are well on the way to being made.
Finally there are the relations of the Canadian service personnel and their dependents with the civilian population in the host country. We have to recognize how important it is for Canada that our men, their wives and children, conduct themselves as Canadian ambassadors. We have to recognize how important it is that the citizens of the host country and those who are taking their place in the bulwarks of freedom there are really working for the same cause. We are not an occupying force, we are not a garrison force. We are there for the same reasons that they have armed forces. This presents a very challenging problem in public relations, both among our forces and with other countries. We are tackling this steadily as best we can.
Now, I thought that the house would like to have me say something about continental defence. This was dealt with though, not

The Address-Mr. Claxton for the first time, on page 3 of the white paper which was issued at the last session, where it was stated:
There has also been a substantial increase in the emphasis on the defence of North America against air attack.
In the last few months there has been a lot of talk in the press and elsewhere about continental defence. The realities of the subject have sometimes been obscured by the sort of Buck Rogerish features like intercontinental pilotless aircraft, long-range guided missiles, flying saucers and even death rays, but the realities are still very real and very serious.
The first talks with the government of the United States on joint defence began in 1938, and ever since then this subject of defence of North America has been under active consideration by representatives of Canada and the United States.
The wartime co-operation between Canada and the United States did not stop with victory. It continued on into the peace. On February 12, 1947 Mr. King made a very important statement on this subject in this chamber. Even at that time military teams of both countries were actively engaged in planning joint defence arrangements including continental air defence. This work was carried out under the chiefs of staff of both countries and was co-ordinated by the permanent joint board on defence. By the beginning of the second war it had become apparent that the continent of North America could be attacked by air.
Almost simultaneously with the development of long-range aircraft came the development of radar capable of making that attack much more difficult. This new device was invented and brought into effective use in Britain. The miracle of radar enabled skilled and courageous airmen to win the battle of Britain.
Effective air defence depends on the organized integration of three sets of operation, each one essential to do the job: first, the detection and identification of the enemy by radar, ground observers or other means; second, communication of this intelligence to a command centre and by that command centre to air and ground anti-aircraft defences and to all the various and important agencies for civil defence; third, aircraft and other anti-aircraft weapons to kill or drive off the attacking bombers.
In any country this is a highly difficult and complicated operation. In any country it is an exceedingly expensive operation. You can imagine that its complexity and expense increase enormously as the size of

the country increases. The area of North America is something between six and seven million square miles, and that fact increases greatly the difficulties and the expense of air defence. We should always remind ourselves that no means has yet been found to make any area so impregnable against air attack that no bombers will get through. Rich as our countries are, the combined resources of Canada and the United States in men, materials and money are not equal to undertake such an immense task even if it were possible.
As in all matters of defence, what we must do is to undertake first what is most urgent and most essential so we can make the best possible use of our resources available for defence. Even before 1947 service planning groups were working on plans for a system of air defence. I can say now one of its principal components was a radar chain across the far north. While such a radar chain might give us early warning of an approaching attack, between this Arctic radar chain and the main radar control system far to the south lay a vast and isolated area in which it was simply not practicable to build the complete gridwork of overlapping radar coverage which is necessary to keep attacking planes under continuous observation. Thus by the time any attackers had travelled the hundreds of miles between the first alarm and the nearest desirable target they would be completely lost to our defending control system.
Therefore such an isolated Arctic radar chain might provide an alarm which might not lead to effective action, while it might nevertheless be likely to immobilize all activities in all target areas. Moreover, it would be very easy to create this result by "spoofing" raids. That is, an enemy aircraft of any size would come in, being very careful indeed to get picked up on a radarscope. The alarm would go out 2,000 miles or 7,000 miles to the south. Activity would stop. The aircraft would either go back home or go in somewhere else. This project never reached the stage of discussion between governments.
There were a number of other developments. Something more than two years ago the two governments agreed to proceed at once to build up a system working upward and outward from the principal target areas, which would give protection to the most vulnerable areas against the most likely forms of attack. On February 25, 1953, for the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), I tabled an exchange of notes covering this operation. Obviously everything that is done in Canada to strengthen

the defence against air attack is done not only for the defence of Canada but, at least equally important, for the defence of targets in the United States. On this account the government and armed forces of the United States have been continuously associated with us in this operation. Arrangements were worked out so the construction and operation of roughly two-thirds of the stations in Canada would be paid for by the United States and one-third by Canada. Work on this project started at once and it has since proceeded expeditiously in accordance with our plans. That is, it has been under way for from two to three years. This system is partly in operation now, and it should be completed in a few months.
Simultaneously with the construction of these radar stations we have gone ahead with the construction of a system of communications embracing a radio relay system supported by land lines and backed up by high frequency radio. We have now largely constructed and partly in operation a military network to provide the necessary communications between the radar screens and the air defenders. You can judge something of the size of the system of communications required for air defence when I tell you that I have been informed that air defence in Britain during the war needed communication services equal to those necessary to carry all civilian traffic in peacetime.
Where existing airfields could be used, we have enlarged and opened them. We have constructed a number of satellite airfields and built emergency landing strips which are necessary in this kind of operation.
Unfortunately there were no aircraft in existence or even under design in any country which had the qualities we consider desirable to meet the threat of air attack across this continent as that threat might develop in the next few years. What was needed was a fighter aircraft with a range twice as great as any fighter in existence. It should have full instrumentation so as to make it useful at night and in all weather and over country presenting great navigational difficulties. It should have a fast rate of climb and good manoeuvrability. It should be able to take off and land using airfields of ordinary length. Finally, it had to carry a large armoury of versatile weapons and be capable of carrying air-to-air missiles when they became available.
These were some of the specifications for the CF-100 to satisfy the foreseen requirements of our own particular problem. It is the conviction of the manufacturers and of the R.C.A.F. that they have been met by the 83276-241
The Address-Mr. Claxton present aircraft. Anyway, it is the only airplane in production anywhere today which can meet anything like our requirements. Indeed, no other country has an aircraft of equivalent performance in production and, so far as I know, we shall be in this position for some considerable time.
Other countries have expressed great interest in the CF-100, and it is not unreasonable to expect that later types of this aircraft will be used much more extensively, particularly as the role of the single-seater fighter comes closer to being met by virtually pilotless aircraft.
Some people seem to think that the contribution of the United States and Canada to the combined forces of the North Atlantic alliance in Europe had to do only with NATO, whereas working together for continental defence had to do only with North America. This is quite wrong, and wrong in two ways. In the first place our experience in two world wars has shown that we have had to go to Europe to fight a war for the defence of our countries, to win victory and to restore peace. Now we are doing the very much more sensible thing of going to Europe in peace so as to make it unnecessary for us to go to Europe in war. Combined defence of Europe under the North Atlantic alliance is defence of North America. North America is the citadel fortress of free peoples and free governments throughout the world. But the bastions of freedom lie also in Britain and France and in all the 14 nations of NATO, and wherever free men stand against the menacing threat of communist imperialism.
In the second place, Canada and the United States are two signatories of the North Atlantic treaty, two partners in the North Atlantic alliance; and like the others we have formally agreed to defend each other's territory. The defence of North America is part of the defence of the North Atlantic region, and Canada and the United States constitute one of the five regional groups of NATO. In the North Atlantic treaty we-that is Canada and the United States-have agreed to plan and build up our joint defence as one of the regional groups of the North Atlantic area.
Far, therefore, from there being any conflict between our work for NATO and our work for continental defence, the two are simply two sides of the same coin, two parts of what, after all, is a world-wide objective, namely the preservation of peace and the defence of our freedom.
It has also sometimes been suggested that continental defence has been subordinated in importance and priority to the build-up of the combined forces of the North Atlantic treaty
384	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Claxton nations in Europe. That is not the case. We -have tried to build up our defences both at home and abroad as fast as both could be effectively done with the resources that were made available. It may be doubted if we could profitably have commenced work on our air defences in North America before we did because the aircraft, the means of communication and the radar equipment which we thought we needed to do this particular job were not even designed, still less in production here or anywhere else.
This job of design, development and production of the equipment for air defence in this country has been most complicated. We needed equipment of entirely new design. The operation was new because of its immense scope, and it raised problems which were new as well as difficult.
The exercises "Signpost", held in 1952, and "Tailwind" in 1953, as well as a number of other exercises, have demonstrated that the equipment has proved better than our expectations. While, of course, it is not 100 per cent effective-no air defence ever is or ever can be-it adds seriously to the hazard of attacking aircraft and so constitutes defence and a deterrent of sufficient importance to justify the large sums of money which it is costing.
As I mentioned, this part-and it is only one part-of the program of joint defence will be completed in 1954, but we are not stopping there. In the United States and here, both independently and in conjunction with the permanent joint board on defence, studies and other work are toeing pressed to find ways and means to improve these defences. The intelligence that the Russians had exploded an atom bomb was naturally a spur to these activities, and the production of additional long-range aircraft and atom bombs or still more destructive bombs increases the threat to North America. In time it might become possible to deliver so devastating an attack on this continent as to seriously cripple its military and industrial strength, actual and potential.
Work on continental defence has included some major research projects. In this, military and scientific experts of Canada and the United States have been working closely together. The reports on these matters are naturally highly secret, but enough has been said officially to indicate something of the magnitude of the requirements and the general character of the far-flung installations which are actually in construction or under consideration. New equipment is being subjected to the most comprehensive tests both technical and by trial in exercises and simu-
TMr. Claxtcn.l

lated operations in which the best of our high-altitude, high-speed aircraft endeavour to penetrate the screens.
Much of this work has been carried on jointly through teams of Canadian and American military and scientific experts, but where they have carried on separately they have kept each other fully informed through the fullest and frankest exchange of information, subject to certain exceptions with regard to atomic information. This autumn there were several of these combined operations going on simultaneously. As a result we have received a report from a joint Canada-United States team engaged on this work, and senior officials representing both countries have had a number of meetings. There has been complete agreement. The chiefs of staff of each country have recommended that this report be acted upon, and the Canadian government has indicated its intention to proceed with this at once.
As the President of the United States said in his address in this chamber on November 14:
In our approach to the problem, we both realize that purest patriotism demands and promotes effective partnership. Thus we evolve joint agreements on all those measures we must jointly undertake to improve the effectiveness of our defences, but every arrangement rests squarely on the sovereign nature of each of our two peoples.
The equipment which is being considered for this new development has been subject to extensive tests. One type of equipment which may be used is known as the "McGill fence", and this was designed, produced and tested in Canada, largely at McGill University. Plans for surveys and production designs for this additional project are already under way and I expect that much of the equipment will be produced in Canada to Canadian design and on Canadian initiative, though what we do will, of course, be undertaken with the full agreement and support of the United States. The new development is intended to increase substantially the likelihood of our having additional time of warning, and also to give us additional assurance against the risks of paralysis through "spoofing".
It should not be thought that this new project is the only matter under study and consideration. At the same time other studies, surveys, research, development and construction are being proceeded with in each country.
To summarize:
1.	Representatives of Canada and the United States have all aspects of continental defence constantly before them for study and action, and the two governments are in general agreement.

2.	Measures recommended by the chiefs of staff on the basis of recent studies have been agreed to, and we are pressing on with surveys and the design and construction of additional defences.
3.	Further work will be considered with a view to agreed action in accordance with the results of studies, surveys, tests and exercises that are under way or that may be undertaken.
4.	As stated in the joint communique issued by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the President on November 14, there is complete agreement on the vital importance of effective methods of joint defence against direct attack.
5.	Experience has shown that the machinery for planning and action for joint defence has worked well, but if any changes appear desirable they will be made.
I have taken this time, Mr. Speaker, to give the house as fully as it is possible to do this account of the background and of the actual stage we have reached with regard to the development of plans and projects for joint defence, and also with regard to the specific development that I have mentioned. This represents another step forward in the co-operation of Canada and the United States to preserve our security and our way of life on this continent as part of the operations of the United Nations and of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The great need and the main problem before us was pointed up by General Gruenther, who is the supreme commander of the allied forces in Europe, when he said:
Never was there a greater need among the NATO nations for unity, for wisdom, and for perseverance. Never was there a greater need to see clearly that our lives are bound inextricably together. Never was there a greater need to continue to work together to build our defensive strength for peace.
He went on to say:
. . . This effort is an international one. It depends ultimately upon the understanding of the peoples we serve that the best-indeed the only-defence for each is the defence of all.
The need for unity of purpose, of will and of action, and determination and perseverance to carry it out has been pointed out on many occasions. It is a challenge to our grand alliance together. Above everything else we should have unity of purpose, agreement and understanding and continued good friendship with our neighbour, the United States,
I was struck, more struck than I have been at any time during the 13 years I have been in this house, with the way in which the Canadian people arrive at essential unity
The Address-Mr. Hees with respect to great purposes, as was shown in this House of Commons yesterday afternoon. It struck me, as it must have struck other hon. members, when I listened to the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), supported as he was so ably, so magnificently, if I may say so, by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), and so well by the leaders of the other parties, how truly the members of this house reflected the feeling of the Canadian people that nothing must come between the United States and Canada which will affect that unity of purpose which is so necessary if we are to preserve our way of life and our security. It is our strongest defence and on it all military defence depends. If it fails in any respect, how could we possibly count with confidence on the 14 nations of NATO standing together?
I am sure the contributions made yesterday will be an added tie in preventing any such failure, and I am sure the relations between Canada and the United States with regard to continental defence and their joint work together for a common purpose will continue to be an example to other nations. I am sure too that these other nations will continue to work with us along the lines indicated by General Gruenther and his great predecessor General Eisenhower as the one way not only to deter aggression but to preserve peace and preserve our security at home and abroad.

speechtext:
Mr. Deputy Speaker, through you I would like to offer my congratulations to the Speaker on his election to his high office, and I would also like to offer my congratulations to you on your appointment. I think both appointments were among the most popular that have been made on parliament hill for quite some time.
This afternoon the matter I want to speak about is one which, although it is not a current problem, is nevertheless a matter which is very important to working people throughout this country, and particularly to municipal governments from coast to coast.
We all know from past experience that the economic pendulum swings both ways, and although today we are enjoying a buoyant economy, I think we must be prepared to look after human needs on a level comparable to Canadian standards of living in case we should be so unfortunate at some future time to be involved in a recession, with its consequent employment difficulties.
If unemployment should increase to a marked degree at some future time, then there are going to be a great many people in this country who will exhaust their unemployment insurance credits, and, through no fault of their own, will be unable to find a job. These people must go on living, and they
366	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Hees cannot do so unless they have the funds to provide food, clothing and shelter for themselves and their families.
These people cannot wait around while this matter is debated in this house, and the buck passed back and forth between various levels of government. I believe we must decide now who is going to bear this burden if conditions should go against us.
For several years now conferences of mayors and reeves throughout this country have been passing resolutions urging this government to accept its responsibilities in this matter, and the reasons they have put forward are five in number.
First, the federal government is the only level of government capable of financing such a program. Today the unemployment insurance fund amounts to nearly one billion dollars, and it continues to grow daily.
Second, the federal government is the only government which has the machinery to administer a program of this kind.
Third, this would avoid the duplication in administration which would occur if various levels of government were attempting to handle this program.
Fourth, uniform standards of assistance would be assured to all Canadians.
Fifth, the limited sources of revenue available to the provinces and municipalities make it impossible for these bodies to meet the financial burden.
I believe these requests by the municipalities to the federal government have been put forward on very logical grounds. They are two in number; first, that the economy of the country is guided to a very large extent by the fiscal policies of the federal government and they, in turn, have a very direct bearing on employment as a whole; second, municipalities simply do not have the sources of revenue necessary to meet this problem when it arises, and the problem must be met when it does arise.
Therefore I urge the government to bring forward legislation at some time in the near future which will assure that people whose unemployment insurance credits have expired, and who through no fault of their own are unable to find jobs, may continue to receive unemployment insurance benefits. I believe we should take this decision now, so the machinery can be put into operation if and when it is ever necessary.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that the measure I have outlined, although it is a necessary one to meet adverse conditions whenever they arise, is of necessity only a negative approach to this problem. The


positive approach is that we should do everything possible to make sure that these adverse conditions do not arise.
I believe the most constructive step this government can take is to give assistance and encouragement to industries to participate in comprehensive and continuing programs of industrial research.
This kind of program, I believe, should have two objectives; first of all, to assist in the development of new sources of cheap power which will attract new industries; second, to provide inducements to industries which will encourage them to develop new and better techniques, which will enable us to process far more of our primary products than we have in the past.
An example of research leading to the possible development of an additional source of cheap power is an investigation into the possibilities of the Passamaquoddy dam project in New Brunswick. This project holds the possibility of an additional million horsepower. The preliminary surveys of this project indicate that it could be economically sound, and that it could provide the maritime provinces with a very important source of cheap power. I believe this government should make available the funds necessary to carry on a thorough investigation to find out if this is or is not a practical project; and if it is discovered to be practical, I believe it should be proceeded with without delay.
We all know that industry goes to power, and if it is possible to develop additional sources of cheap power in the maritime provinces, then industries will locate there, and that will make the economy of the maritimes far less dependent on the primary products which they produce. To me, Mr. Speaker, this is the only practical way I know to effectively decentralize industry. We hear many speeches urging and agreeing with the idea of decentralization of industry. This, I think, is a practical approach to the problem.
Now I should like to deal with an example of research leading to the development of new industries, which I think could take the form of assistance given to the potential oil and gas by-products industry in western Canada. We all know that in Alberta, and to a lesser extent in British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, we have enormous resources of gas and oil. In recent years more than $5 billion of these reserves have been proved up, and we know that we have discovered only a small fraction of the reserves which are confidently believed to be present.
If the incentive for exploration is continued by the opening up of additional markets for these products, and if that expansion is

accompanied by a comprehensive and continuing program of industrial research to develop better techniques for the processing of oil and gas by-products, then I think we can develop in western Canada a by-products industry which will be of tremendous importance to the economy of the Canadian west.
This will lead to the building of literally dozens of sulphur, chemical and petrochemical plants, which will require hundreds of millions of dollars by way of capital investment and will create employment for many thousands of Canadians. Not only will it provide employment for Canadians, but I believe an expansion of this kind can be the solution to our immigration problem. It will enable us to bring in many people of the right type from other lands to contribute to our progress and welfare in this country; because with expanding industry, those who come in will not be jostling Canadians out of jobs. They will simply be taking their places beside Canadians to make this a more productive land.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that if the oil and gas industry is given freedom to grow and to expand, and if the potential byproducts industry is assisted by a progressive, comprehensive and continuing program of research, there can be developed in western Canada a very important steel industry, which would utilize Canadian iron ore as well as Canadian coal and gas. This industry could produce steel pipe and steel casings to be used in thousands of Canadian oil wells and in thousands of miles of Canadian oil pipe lines across the prairie provinces.
I have mentioned only a couple of possible steps which this government could take to assist in maintaining the present high level of employment and increasing that level of employment very materially. When we consider the tremendous natural resources of this country, from coast to coast, I think we must all agree that our best chance of maintaining a high level of employment, and of increasing it materially, is to develop our vast natural resources instead of just sitting around talking about them and thinking about them.
We in this country are living in a time when our very survival depends upon our ability to trade with other free nations. The failure of the democratic countries to do so is simply going to drive many countries into the orbit of communism.
In our pursuit of unclogging the channels of trade we must be prepared, in the very near future, to compete on a much more
The Address-Mr. Shaw highly competitive basis, both at home and abroad. The reason for this is that wage levels throughout the world are by no means uniform. We are proud that in Canada our wage level is considerably higher than the average. If we are to successfully compete with the many low-wage countries with whom we are soon going to have to compete, the only way we can do so is to considerably increase our technical know-how. That is the only way we can possibly lower our costs of production, and bring those costs down to a point at least somewhere near the costs of production of the people with whom we are competing.
At the present time there stands on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) a resolution calling for the setting up of a committee of the house, to consist of members of parliament from all parties, as well as representative of labour, industry, agriculture and education, to sit down and see what results can be expected from a very important and accelerated program of industrial research.
I hope this resolution will be debated in the house on a non-partisan basis, because I feel it is something we should all support. The work of that committee should bring into sharp focus the urgent need at the present time for industrial research.
I said at the beginning of my remarks that I believe a continuation of unemployment insurance benefits is very necessary if adverse conditions at some future time should make it impossible for people, whose unemployment insurance credits have expired, to find jobs. However, I think we all appreciate the fact that the only real unemployment insurance is an increasingly high level of employment. The people of Canada want jobs, not handouts.
I sincerely hope the government will give some consideration to the suggestions I have made today, because I think they would assist in making an increasingly high level of employment a reality.

Mr. Speaker, while I am tempted at this time to devote my remarks to those matters which are of peculiar concern to my own constituency, my present intention is to confine what I have to say almost exclusively to the amendments.
I must confess there is a temptation to take advantage of this opportunity to deal with coal, because actually there is a serious problem in connection with the coal industry. I am tempted to deal with agriculture, particularly the marketing aspect of the problem. There is a temptation to deal with old age

The Address-Mr. Shaw pensions and, as I say, with a multitude of problems affecting the people not only in my province but throughout Canada. [DOT]
Despite the fact that on August 10 a minority of the Canadian electorate did reelect a Liberal government, there are still problems. I am sure some of those who were led to believe that the Liberal party held the solution to all problems now fully realize the extent to which at least in some respects they were deluded.
The section of the subamendment with which we are particularly concerned is as follows:
We further represent that this house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to recommend legislation establishing a nation-wide health insurance program, with provision for provincial participation.
Last session, on November 24, 1952, to be exact, the C.C.F. moved a similar amendment to the amendment. While similar, it did differ in some respects. That amendment of November 24, 1952, reads as follows:
That the amendment be amended by deleting paragraphs (d) and (e) and by substituting therefor the following:
"We regret further that Your Excellency's advisers have failed:
(a)	to recommend legislation establishing a nation-wide health insurance program, with provision for provincial administration;
(b)	to implement their proposals to the dominion-provincial conference of 1945."
I cannot of course fully comprehend the true significance of changing the word "administration" as it appeared in the 1952 amendment, and substituting therefor the word "participation". I realize of course that the mover of the amendment to the amendment did emphasize the fact that under a scheme such as he envisaged administration would be on the provincial level and from there pass along as far as possible to the health units, and I presume he meant municipalities within the provinces.
As I say, I cannot comprehend the full significance of the dropping of the word "administration" and the substitution therefor of the word "participation". Consequently I cannot fully comprehend the significance of their dropping section (b) which, as I have already indicated, called for the implementation of the proposals of the dominion-provincial conference of 1945.
There is one other significant difference between the proposal of 1953 and the proposal of 1952. The mover of the amendment to the amendment last year, on November 24, said first of all, "We think that the plan must be contributory". I find a departure

from that position this year at page 55 of Hansard for November 16, 1953. I quote:
Finally, we believe that the plan should be financed by the federal government out of the general revenue of Canada.
As I say, I cannot at the moment fully comprehend the significance of the change. However, I think it is sufficient to say- and I say it in the best possible spirit-that there is a good deal of evidence that the C.C.F. are coming closer and closer to the position which the Social Crediters have taken over the years with respect to this matter. At the same time that they are coming closer and closer to our position, they are moving farther and farther from their former position which I have always feared embraced that which is frequently designated as state medicine. They may -call this state medicine, I do not know; but of course my understanding of state medicine is something a good deal different from that program enunciated by the leader of the C.C.F. on November 16.
When we endorsed that subamendment last year we made it perfectly clear that our endorsation did not commit us in any way whatsoever to the acceptance of any specific health plan or program which they might have in mind. Second, our support of the amendment to the amendment last year simply indicated, as we made clear, our belief that an expanded health program for Canada is desirable and undoubtedly is necessary.
Our position is exactly the same at this time. Our attitude toward this whole problem of health revolves around several important beliefs which we hold. I think it was last year, Mr. Speaker, that my leader made the declaration on our behalf that in our opinion there is no greater asset to any nation than the health of its people. He also pointed out-and I repeat our position with respect to these principles-that every effort should be made, first by the people individually-and let me underline that-and collectively through their governments to achieve a high standard of national wellbeing.
Government activities in the field of health, Mr. Speaker, should not, in my estimation, be limited only to financial participation and possibly to a measure of administration. I believe government participation must be directed to the creation of conditions within the country under which individuals are provided with the opportunity of securing a decent standard of living; because, as far as we are concerned, one of the most certain steps toward better health would be, I repeat, the establishment

of economic conditions which would provide an opportunity for our people to acquire a decent standard of living, which of course includes a decent standard of food, clothing and housing.
We shall never forget, when referring to that aspect of the whole question, that during world war II between 40 and 50 per cent of our young Canadian men and women who either reported voluntarily for military service or who were called up under the N.R.M.A. were rejected on physical grounds. We cannot but believe that that situation could be traced back, without any difficulty whatsoever, to the conditions of the 1930's while they were young people growing up.
We think any health program in this country should have a definite objective. This is not new. We have stated this objective before. It is very close to the statement made by the sponsor of the amendment to the amendment. As I say, we have made it in the house over the years; and it is to make it possible for every Canadian, irrespective of means, to obtain medical, dental, optical and hospital services, and along with them a sound program of health education, with emphasis upon preventive medicine. Any scheme one may contemplate must ensure, among other things, that there are sufficient doctors, technicians, clinics, hospital beds, nurses and dentists.
May I say just at this point that sometimes when we hear certain persons referring to matters of this kind they either intentionally or unintentionally leave the impression that nothing or at least not much is being done in this field. All I have to do is remind hon. members that in many of the provinces of Canada the local governments have been acutely aware of the need for increased facilities and increased personnel.
The federal government in recent years has made money available for such things as hospital construction. As I say, they too are aware of the needs. All one has to do is examine the statistics in order to learn that at least in many parts of Canada we are moving rapidly forward in the acquisition of hospital facilities, etc.
There is one problem which crops up frequently, the apparent desire on the part of doctors to practise in the larger urban centres where modern facilities are available and where they are able to carry on their profession much more successfully. I cannot remember the source of my information, but I recall reading an article recently which set out a method by which we could encourage young doctors to practise in the rural areas. Young students desirous of entering medical
The Address-Mr. Shaw school could be given financial assistance, and this could be done under a provision that if the doctor would practise at a country point for one year a certain part of the loan would be cancelled and if he practised for two years a more substantial part would be cancelled.
The suggestion appealed to me for two reasons, one of which is the tragedy of many young students who are desirous of entering the medical profession but who must discard the idea because of the financial cost involved.
In any scheme or health insurance program it is imperative, as far as we are concerned, that five vital principles be recognized and maintained. First, as I have indicated, we feel that there should be a fair measure of individual responsibility. It is amazing what a fair measure of individual responsibility will do.
I am reminded of the time I was teaching school in a certain area a number of years ago, and I was presented with the opportunity as a non-taxpayer of acquiring municipal hospitalization for $5 a year. We were approximately 35 miles from the nearest municipal hospital. I assume it is quite natural for members of the medical profession to prefer to treat patients in a hospital rather than some point 40 miles away and the result was that many persons who should not have been hospitalized were hospitalized. It was also quite certain that many people were being hospitalized on their own initiative. Of course that meant their doctor had to be prevailed upon to agree that they should be hospitalized.
But all this created a situation which simply could not be continued, namely the facilities being jammed to overflowing. Shortly after that they brought in a proviso that each patient would have to pay $1 a day, and almost overnight that problem which had existed in that particular area was solved. Quite apart from all this, I hold a rather deep conviction that our objective should not be to remove from the shoulders of any individual all semblance of responsibility with respect to this or many other things to which we might refer.
If I recall correctly the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who moved the amendment to the amendment, contended that patients should have a choice of doctors. Certainly that should continue to be the case. I think that is a rather pronounced departure on the part of the C.C.F.

That may be true, but we are seeking a solution to the problem. I think we should want something better. I think all of us believe in freedom. We expect to be free within the accepted sense of the word today. We should be free as long as we recognize that other people should be free too. Surely if that is the case we must be logical and accept the principle that other groups within our society shall be free also. We submit that any scheme must guarantee that there shall be no regimentation of patients, doctors, nurses or hospitals.
The third point which we submit should characterize any scheme, if you want to use that rather bad word, is that emphasis must be placed on preventive medicine, in other words we should try to keep people well. I do not say this in a critical sense at all, but I have made rather a comprehensive study of certain health insurance schemes in operation in various pa-rts of the world and it seems to me, if I can accept the information which I have procured from various sources, that adequate emphasis is not placed On the preventive aspect of medicine. In trying to meet the needs of people who are unwell or who require treatment of a curative nature they have allowed the preventive aspect of medicine to be pretty well brushed aside. We say that whatever program of this kind comes into existence in the provinces or in Canada should recognize the value of preventive medicine.
Fourth, we consider that any proposed scheme must operate with the co-operation of the federal, provincial and municipal governments. One might go beyond that and suggest that it must include voluntary health organizations, health units, etc. We feel, as apparently does the mover, that the administration of any such scheme should be on the provincial and municipal levels. We feel strongly about that matter, Mr. Speaker. We are absolutely opposed to the imposition upon the people of this country of any scheme which gives some indication that it may destroy the existing patient-doctor relationship. We should not like to see-in fact, we would be very much opposed to them-some things which are apparently being done under certain schemes elsewhere where, in the final

analysis, laymen are the ones who dictate as to the type of treatment which an ill person should receive.
There is evidence of that situation in several of the schemes overseas. I may be wrong but I believe that, in the powers vested in the local executive councils in the scheme in Britain, there is a strong indication that laymen are having far too much to say about the type of treatment which the individual might secure. We never would support any proposition or scheme which places treatment on the assembly-line basis or, in other words, simply the pushing of patients through, with no opportunity whatsoever to deal with the psychological implications of individual cases. Any medical man will tell you that those are extremely important in dealing with people who are ill, whether they are really ill or ill in an imaginary sense. I think also that it is extremely important that we recognize that in the development of any scheme we must proceed with sufficient care to have a reasonable guarantee that inflated demands which follow the implementation of any set of proposals shall not create a situation where we are worse off than we were before we started. As I say in connection with that point, this matter of the maintenance of individual responsibility certainly will play an important part.
I do not desire to take too much of the time of the house, Mr. Speaker. I am conscious of the fact that the membership of the house is anxious to have at least one vote today. I am, of course, fully conscious of the fact that I shall have further opportunity to say other things that I should like to say. I mentioned some of them earlier and certainly it is my intention to take advantage of the opportunities provided to me to give voice to my opinions with regard to some of the major problems confronting us.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I make it absolutely clear that, when we support this amendment to the amendment, we do not want it to be construed that our endorsation of that subamendment commits us to the acceptance or the support of any specific plan which the C.C.F. may now or later advance. We have our own ideas with respect to that matter. As I said before, our endorsation of the subamendment simply indicates our belief that an expanded health program for Canada is desirable and essential. Being an Albertan, I think we in Alberta have made great strides. We should certainly like to see the federal government come along with financing more financial assistance. I am sure that we can advance even more

rapidly than in the past. I do not want to leave the impression-and I have made certain of that already-that the federal government is doing nothing. I realize that they are. I am conscious of the grants for hospital construction, et cetera. Mr. Speaker, we are supporting the subamendment subject to those considerations just indicated.
